title: Explain a slow or fast E2 from the chair
asks: One stereoisomer eliminates far more slowly (or faster) than the others. Explain in detail.

know.h: The requirement. In {{E2}} the hydrogen and the leaving group must be anti-periplanar. The C-H electrons push in from behind the C-LG bond, like the back-side attack of {{SN2}}. This gives the best orbital overlap, the most stable transition state and the fastest reaction.
Syn-periplanar (H and leaving group on the same side) has poorer overlap and a less stable transition state, so it does not compete.
On a cyclohexane, anti-periplanar means trans-diaxial: an axial leaving group and an axial hydrogen on the carbon next to it.
An equatorial leaving group has no anti hydrogen. Anti to an equatorial bond lies a C-C bond of the ring. Both hydrogens on the next carbon are gauche to it.
The ring flip exchanges axial and equatorial on every carbon at once. It never changes which face (up or down) a group is on.

Trans neighbours are both axial or both equatorial. Cis neighbours are one axial and one equatorial. So a hydrogen on C2 can be anti to a leaving group on C1 only if that hydrogen is trans to the leaving group, which means the substituent on C2 is cis to it.
Axial groups cost energy: methyl 1.74 kcal/mol (K = 19.5), ethyl 1.79, isopropyl 2.61 (K = 86.0), tert-butyl 5.5 (K = 11,916). K is the ratio of the equatorial chair to the axial chair.

The rate follows the reactive chair. Only molecules in the chair with the leaving group axial (and an axial H next door) can react. If that chair is the stable one, {{E2}} is fast. If it is rare, {{E2}} is slow. If it does not exist, {{E2}} hardly happens at all.

A tert-butyl group locks the ring with itself equatorial: about 1 molecule in 12,000 has it axial. A leaving group cis to a 4-tert-butyl group is held axial; a leaving group trans to it is held equatorial.

The exam example. The all-trans isomer of 1,2,3,4,5,6-hexachlorocyclohexane has every Cl equatorial. After the flip every Cl is axial but every H is equatorial. Neither chair has an axial Cl next to an axial H, so it reacts 7000 times more slowly than any other stereoisomer.
Stereoisomers share everything else: same base, same leaving group, same kind of carbon. So the explanation of a rate difference between them is always the geometry, shown on the chair.

Skill: a full-credit answer has four parts. State the anti-periplanar (trans-diaxial) requirement, draw the chair or chairs, say what is anti to the leaving group in each, and compare with the other isomer.

method: Write the requirement first: H and leaving group anti-periplanar, which on a ring means trans-diaxial on neighbouring carbons.
Draw both chairs of the slow isomer and label the leaving group axial or equatorial in each.
In the chair with the leaving group axial, check the axial position on each neighbouring carbon: hydrogen or substituent?
Decide which case it is: no chair has an axial leaving group next to an axial hydrogen (E2 blocked), or the chair that has them is the unstable one (E2 slow, and say how unstable using the A-values).
Do the same for the fast isomer and point to its axial leaving group and the axial hydrogen next to it.
Finish with one sentence that compares the two isomers.

pitfalls.h: Writing only "steric hindrance". The reason is the missing anti-periplanar hydrogen, and the chair has to show it.
Looking at one chair only. The grader wants to see that the ring flip does not help, or why the flipped chair is rare.
Saying the ring flip moves a group to the other face. Up stays up: only axial and equatorial change.
Saying an equatorial Cl is too stable to leave. The point is that no hydrogen is anti to it.
Explaining the slow isomer and never saying why the other isomers are fast.
